blocks.text: How to Answer Any Behavior Question

Now, you might be thinking... "Hang on, Biron! What about answering all those behavioral questions? You're just going to leave me on my own?" Not quite. Here's what I recommend. These questions can be stressful to answer, but the best way to keep your nerves under control is to follow a pre-planned answer formula. I recommend the S.T.A.R. method: Situation. Task. Action. Result. Use it every time you hear behavioral questions (questions starting with phrases like "tell me about a situation where you had to ___."
First describe the situation. You need to paint a clear picture or the rest of your story won't make sense. When was this story? Who else was involved? What was the basic situation?
Next, what was the task or challenge you had to overcome? What was the goal?
Now, what action or strategy did you use? What steps did you choose to overcome the problem orachieve the goal, and why?

Finally, the result. How did things turn out? And what did you learn from this experience that you continue to use? Employers love seeing that you're always trying to improve and learn from challenges. If you follow this method, you'll stay on-track with your answers and feel calmer. Remember to practice at home, though. Get very familiar with these 4 steps.
The STAR method, step by step.
Use this framework for any question that starts with "Tell me about a time" or "Give an example of."
Set the scene in one or two sentences: where, when, what was at stake
Explain your specific responsibility or goal
Describe the steps you personally took, using "I" not "we"
Add what you learned or would do differently
"Tell me about a time you improved a process."

S: Our squadron's parts requests took an average of six days. T: As supply supervisor, I had to cut delays before deployment. A: I mapped the process, removed two duplicate approvals, and trained 12 people on the new steps. R: Wait time dropped to two days, a 66% improvement, and readiness rose 9%.

blocks.text: 1. "Tell me about a time you faced a conflict on a team. How did you handle that?" 2. "Tell me about a time you failed. How did you deal with this situation?" 3. "Tell me about how you prioritize things" 4. "Tell me about your proudest professional accomplishment" 5. "Describe a time when you were not satisfied with your performance. What happened? 6. "Describe a time you had to make a decision without all the information" 7. "Tell me about a long-term project you managed. How did you keep everything organized? 8. "Give me an example of an important goal you set in the past and how you reached it" 9. "Tell me a time you had to be relatively quick in coming to a decision" 10. "Tell me about the first job you ever had. What did you do to learn the ropes?" 11. "Tell me about how you make decisions, with an example" 12. "Describe a crisis you faced at work. What was your role? How did you resolve it?" 13. "Describe a time when you were asked to do something you weren’t trained to do. How did you adapt?" 14. "Describe a time you had to think on your feet to solve a problem" 15. "Give me an example of a time you had to explain something fairly complex to someone. How did you make sure they understood you?"
Answer every "tell me about a time" with STAR.
Situation, Task, Action, Result. Spend most of your answer on Action and Result, and use numbers wherever you can.

blocks.q: Tell me about a time you faced a conflict on a team.
blocks.a: What they want to know: How you handle disagreements. How to answer: Set the scene briefly, explain your role, the steps you took to resolve it, and the outcome. Veteran tip: Show collaboration and listening, not just authority.

blocks.q: Describe a time you failed.
blocks.a: What they want to know: Accountability and learning. How to answer: Own the mistake, explain what you changed, and share the better result that followed. Veteran tip: Choose a real, recoverable failure.

blocks.q: Tell me about a time you led a team.
blocks.a: What they want to know: Leadership style. How to answer: Give team size, goal, how you motivated people, and a measurable result. Veteran tip: Translate rank into team size and scope.

blocks.q: Give an example of a goal you reached.
blocks.a: What they want to know: Drive and planning. How to answer: Explain the goal, your plan, obstacles, and the measurable result. Veteran tip: Inspections, certifications, and readiness goals are strong examples.

blocks.q: Describe a time you went above and beyond.
blocks.a: What they want to know: Initiative. How to answer: Show what was expected, what you did beyond it, and why it mattered. Veteran tip: Awards can support your story; explain what they were for.

blocks.q: Tell me about a time you made a decision with incomplete information.
blocks.a: What they want to know: Judgment. How to answer: Explain the risk, how you gathered what you could, your decision, and the result. Veteran tip: Military decision-making translates very well here.

blocks.q: Describe a time you had to adapt to change.
blocks.a: What they want to know: Flexibility. How to answer: Show the change, how you adjusted, and how you helped others adjust. Veteran tip: PCS moves and mission changes are relatable examples.

blocks.q: Tell me about a time you improved a process.
blocks.a: What they want to know: Continuous improvement. How to answer: Describe the old process, your change, and the measured improvement. Veteran tip: Quantify time, cost, or error reduction.

blocks.q: Describe a time you managed multiple priorities.
blocks.a: What they want to know: Organization. How to answer: Explain how you prioritized, communicated, and delivered. Veteran tip: Mention tools or systems you used to track tasks.

blocks.q: Tell me about a time you handled a difficult person.
blocks.a: What they want to know: Interpersonal skill. How to answer: Stay professional; show empathy, boundaries, and a resolution. Veteran tip: Avoid criticizing former leaders.

blocks.q: Give an example of mentoring someone.
blocks.a: What they want to know: Developing others. How to answer: Describe the person, the gap, how you coached, and their result. Veteran tip: Sailors, soldiers, or airmen you trained and promoted make great stories.

blocks.q: Describe a time you received tough feedback.
blocks.a: What they want to know: Coachability. How to answer: Share the feedback, your response, and what improved. Veteran tip: Show growth, not defensiveness.

blocks.q: Tell me about a high-pressure situation.
blocks.a: What they want to know: Composure under stress. How to answer: Describe the stakes, your actions, and the outcome. Veteran tip: Keep details unclassified and civilian-friendly.

blocks.q: Describe a time you worked with a diverse team.
blocks.a: What they want to know: Inclusion and collaboration. How to answer: Show how you leveraged different perspectives to succeed. Veteran tip: Joint and coalition teams are excellent examples.

blocks.q: Tell me about your proudest accomplishment.
blocks.a: What they want to know: What you value. How to answer: Pick one that aligns with the job and share the impact. Veteran tip: Tie it to the skills the employer needs most.

blocks.q: How much is the VA funding fee?
blocks.a: For a first-time VA purchase loan it is 2.15% of the loan with less than 5% down, 1.5% with 5% or more down, and 1.25% with 10% or more down. After first use it is 3.3% with less than 5% down. Veterans receiving VA disability compensation are generally exempt.

blocks.q: Does BAH count as income for a VA loan?
blocks.a: Yes. Lenders generally count Basic Allowance for Housing as income for active duty borrowers when it is expected to continue.

blocks.q: How does VA combine disability ratings?
blocks.a: VA applies each rating to the remaining "whole person" from highest to lowest instead of adding them, then rounds to the nearest 10%. For example, 50% and 30% combine to 65, which rounds to 70%.

blocks.q: What is the Active Duty Veteran and Hometown Hero Home-Owners Club?
blocks.a: We are a 501(c)(3) nonprofit based in Temecula, California (EIN 84-3348125). We give active duty service members, veterans, military families, and hometown heroes free education on home buying, VA benefits, and careers, and we donate to local charities in Southern California.

blocks.q: Who do you serve?
blocks.a: Active duty members of all six branches (Army, Navy, Air Force, Marine Corps, Coast Guard, and Space Force), veterans, Guard and Reserve members, military spouses, and hometown heroes such as firefighters, law enforcement, EMTs, nurses, and teachers. Our local focus is San Diego, Riverside, Orange, and Los Angeles counties, and our online resources serve every state.

blocks.q: Are your workshops and webinars free?
blocks.a: Yes. Our webinars and resource guides are free and come with no obligation.

blocks.q: What is a VA home loan?
blocks.a: A VA home loan is a mortgage partly guaranteed by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. Eligible service members, veterans, and some surviving spouses can usually buy a home with no down payment and no private mortgage insurance, subject to lender approval.

blocks.q: How do I get my VA Certificate of Eligibility (COE)?
blocks.a: You can request your COE online at VA.gov, ask a VA-approved lender to pull it for you, or apply by mail. Our free VA Home Buying Webinar walks you through each option.

blocks.q: Where can I get help right now if I'm in crisis?
blocks.a: Call the Veterans Crisis Line at 988 and press 1, text 838255, or chat online at VeteransCrisisLine.net. It is free, confidential, and available 24/7.

blocks.q: How can I support your mission?
blocks.a: Donate through PayPal from this page. As a 501(c)(3) nonprofit, gifts may be tax-deductible as allowed by law. You can also volunteer or share our resources with someone who served.

blocks.text: Bigger property tax savings for 100% disabled veteran homeowners.

Signed September 28, 2026 (Chapter 727, Statutes of 2026), SB 296 expands California's Disabled Veterans' Exemption. Starting with the January 1, 2027 lien date, a qualifying veteran can exempt half, or all, of the first $1 million of their home's value from property tax.
50% of the first $1 million of your home's value exempt. That is up to $500,000 off your taxable value.
100% of the first $1 million exempt if household income is $83,474 or less (2027 limit, adjusted yearly).
2027 to 2031 Applies to lien dates January 1, 2027 through 2031, starting with the 2027-28 tax bill. Set to expire January 1, 2032 unless extended.
How it compares to the current exemption
50% of value, up to $1 million (up to $500,000 off)
If your home is assessed at $371,778 or less and your income is above the low-income limit, you keep the current exemption, which is the better deal at that value.

Example: on a home assessed at $700,000, the current basic exemption removes $185,889 from taxable value. Under SB 296 it removes $350,000. At California's 1% base rate, that is about $3,500 a year off the base tax instead of about $1,860. If household income is under the limit, the full $700,000 is exempt. Local bonds and assessments vary, so your actual savings will differ.
California veterans rated 100% disabled from a service-connected condition, or paid at the 100% rate through Individual Unemployability (TDIU) .
Veterans who are blind in both eyes or have lost the use of two or more limbs because of service.
Unmarried surviving spouses of a veteran who qualified, or who died of a service-connected cause. The veteran must have been a California resident on January 1 of the year of death.
The home must be your principal residence , owned by the veteran, the spouse, or both. A veteran in a hospital or care facility can still qualify if the home is not rented out.
You cannot combine it with the homeowners' exemption or another exemption on the same home.
Get your VA rating decision letter. It must show 100% service-connected or TDIU and the effective date. Download a benefit summary letter at VA.gov, and keep a copy of your DD-214.
Get Form BOE-261-G , Claim for Disabled Veterans' Property Tax Exemption, from your county assessor (links below). It is filed with the county, not the state.
Applying for the low-income level? Also complete the county's household income worksheet. Low-income claims must be filed every year by February 15 .
Surviving spouses also include the marriage certificate, the veteran's death certificate, and a DIC letter if you have one.

File as soon as you qualify. The basic exemption is a one-time filing that stays in place while you remain eligible. Late claims usually receive a partial exemption (85% in many counties) for the first year. If your VA rating is retroactive, ask about prior-year refunds. San Diego County applies them up to 8 years back.
Already have the exemption? Call your county assessor's disabled veterans unit and ask how your 2027 exemption will be recalculated under SB 296, and whether you need to file anything new.
Report changes. Tell the assessor if you sell, move, or your rating changes. Missing this can bring a 25% penalty.
Tip: Counties are still publishing SB 296 procedures for the 2027 tax year. Confirm the details with your county assessor before you file. Your County Veterans Service Office can help for free.

blocks.q: What is California SB 296?
blocks.a: SB 296 is a 2026 California law (Chapter 727, signed September 28, 2026) that expands the property tax exemption for 100% disabled veteran homeowners. Starting with the January 1, 2027 lien date, qualifying veterans can exempt 50% of the first $1 million of their home's value, or 100% of the first $1 million if household income is $83,474 or less. It runs through 2031 unless extended.

blocks.q: Who qualifies for the SB 296 disabled veteran property tax exemption?
blocks.a: California homeowners who are rated 100% disabled from a service-connected condition or paid at the 100% rate through Individual Unemployability (TDIU), or who are blind in both eyes or have lost the use of two or more limbs from service. Certain unmarried surviving spouses also qualify. The home must be your principal residence.

blocks.q: How do I apply for the disabled veterans property tax exemption in California?
blocks.a: File Form BOE-261-G, Claim for Disabled Veterans' Property Tax Exemption, with your county assessor. Include your VA rating decision letter showing 100% or TDIU and the effective date, plus your DD-214. Low-income claimants also file a household income worksheet each year by February 15.

blocks.q: When does SB 296 take effect?
blocks.a: The new exemption applies to the January 1, 2027 lien date, which is the 2027-28 property tax bill, and continues for lien dates through 2031.

blocks.q: I already have the disabled veterans exemption. Do I need to reapply?
blocks.a: Counties are still publishing their SB 296 procedures. Call your county assessor's disabled veterans unit to confirm whether your exemption will be recalculated automatically for 2027 or whether you need to file anything new. Low-income claimants must still file every year.

blocks.q: Can I combine this with the homeowners' exemption?
blocks.a: No. The disabled veterans exemption replaces the $7,000 homeowners' exemption on the same home. You cannot receive both.

blocks.q: What is HUD-VASH?
blocks.a: HUD-VASH (HUD-Veterans Affairs Supportive Housing, often called VASH) pairs a HUD rental voucher with VA case management to help veterans who are homeless find and keep permanent housing. Start by calling the National Call Center for Homeless Veterans at 877-424-3838 or your local VA medical center.

blocks.q: What happened to VASP?
blocks.a: VA ended the VA Servicing Purchase (VASP) program in May 2025. In 2026 VA launched a Partial Claim Program to help veterans with VA loans who are behind on payments. Call a VA loan technician at 877-827-3702 or visit VA.gov to learn your options.

blocks.q: I am behind on rent or about to lose my housing. What should I do?
blocks.a: Call 877-424-3838 right away. Supportive Services for Veteran Families (SSVF) can help with rent, deposits, utilities, and moving costs to keep you housed or rehouse you quickly.

blocks.q: How do I get help with my electric, gas, or water bill in California?
blocks.a: Apply for LIHEAP through your local community action agency, enroll in CARE or FERA with your utility for an ongoing discount, and ask about Medical Baseline if you use medical equipment at home. Dial 211 for local programs.

blocks.q: Are there grants for veterans who need emergency money?
blocks.a: Yes. Operation Homefront, USA Cares, VFW Unmet Needs, and each branch relief society offer emergency grants or zero-interest loans. Eligibility varies by program.

blocks.q: Where can I get free help filing for VA benefits?
blocks.a: Your County Veterans Service Office, DAV, and other accredited service organizations file claims for free. You never have to pay to file a VA claim.

blocks.text: The way you dress for a job interview tells potential employers a lot about you. The right interview outfit conveys an understanding of the company culture and professional environments in general and shows that you respect the hiring manager and want to make a good impression.
Have an interview outfit ready to go, so you're prepared to interview at a moment's notice. You’ll feel comfortable, confident, and ready to shine.

Reread the job posting and analyze it to determine what the employer is looking for in a candidate. Then make a list of the skills, knowledge, professional, and personal qualities that are required by the employer and are most important for success in the job. Be ready to describe the attributes that make you the perfect match for the job. The closer your qualifications match the job requirements, the better chance you'll have of getting a second-round interview and a job offer.
How much do you know about the company that you're interviewing with? Before you go to the interview be sure you're well informed.

Research the company by reading their website, looking at their social media presence, reviewing LinkedIn profiles of current and past employees, and talking to any personal connections who’ve worked at the company. Pay special attention to the job skills most common among employees and any mention of the company culture. Culture fit is important – for your happiness, as well as for the employer’s success.

Don’t forget to do a Google News search to find out whether the company has received any positive or negative press recently. You might learn about initiatives that make the company a more attractive employer or you might learn that the organization is in trouble and you’d be better off focusing your attention elsewhere.

Want to boost your chances of getting hired? Get a referral from a networking connection. Contacts who work for the company (or used to work there and left on good terms) can give you the inside track to getting the job. Hiring managers often prefer to interview candidates who come recommended rather than those who apply online. Your contact can also tell you more about the hiring process at the employer, which will make it easier to navigate than if you come in without insider knowledge.

Taking the time to review typical interview questions will help give you a framework for your responses. It will also reduce stress because you won't be scrambling for an answer during the interview. Practice interviewing with a friend or family member ahead of time, and it will be much easier when you're actually in a job interview.

A job interview gives you a chance to shine. What you say and what you do is going to either move you to the next round of consideration for employment or knock you out of contention for the job. The more you know about successful interview techniques, the smoother the interview will go. If you're one of those people, and it happens to almost everyone, who gets really anxious about interviews, there are coping strategies you can use to help minimize stress.

Is it okay to bring a cup of coffee or your cell phone to the interview? How should you greet the interviewer? And what should you bring with you to the meeting – just yourself, or your resume and cover letter, or a complete copy of your application including portfolio? Brush up on proper interview etiquette before you go and avoid being caught wrongfooted during the conversation.

It's important to know where you need to go for your job interview. You don't want to be late or arrive out of breath and flustered. Use Google Maps to get directions if you're not sure where you are going. Program your GPS, if you have one, so you can find the best route to the company. Check on parking and/or public transportation, so you arrive with time to spare. Consider doing a test run the day before to make sure you have the right directions.

It's important to know what to bring to a job interview — a portfolio with extra copies of your resume, a list of references, and questions you have for the interviewer. Be sure you have everything you need ready to go. If you’re job searching in earnest, it’s a good idea to prepare a bag with all your materials so that you can be ready to interview whenever an opportunity arises.

Taking the time to say thank you after a job interview not only is good interview etiquette, it reinforces your interest in the position. Your thank-you letter is also an opportunity to address any issues or concerns that came up during the interview. It may even serve as a second chance to emphasize your qualifications.
Walk in ready. Walk out remembered.
A complete, step-by-step checklist from the week before to the thank-you note. Print it or save it to your phone.
Reread the job posting and highlight the top five requirements
Research the company: mission, products, customers, recent news
Look up your interviewers on LinkedIn
Prepare five STAR stories that prove those requirements
Translate every military term in your stories into plain English
Write three questions to ask them
Confirm the date, time, time zone, and format (phone, video, or in person)
Plan your route and parking, or test your camera, mic, and internet
Choose and try on your outfit; get it cleaned and pressed
Print 3 copies of your resume and a list of references
Arrive 10 minutes early, or log in 5 minutes early
Bring a notepad, pen, resume copies, and your questions
Firm handshake, eye contact, and a smile
Listen fully before you answer; it is fine to pause and think
Open with a 60-second "tell me about yourself" that ends on why this job
Use numbers: team size, budget, results, percentages
Answer behavioral questions with Situation, Task, Action, Result
Connect each answer back to their needs
Close by restating your interest and asking about next steps
Send a personal thank-you email to each interviewer
Mention one specific thing you discussed
Write down the questions you were asked for next time
Log the interview and next follow-up date in your tracker
Know your clearance level, investigation type, and date
Never discuss classified details; describe work at an unclassified level
Have your SF-86 history handy for any follow-up paperwork

blocks.q: How early should I arrive for an interview?
blocks.a: Plan to arrive 10 to 15 minutes early for in-person interviews and log in 5 minutes early for video interviews. Arriving much earlier can put pressure on the employer.

blocks.q: What should a veteran wear to a civilian interview?
blocks.a: Match or slightly exceed the company dress code. Business professional is the safe default for corporate and government roles. Keep it clean, pressed, and simple; skip unit pins or uniform items unless the employer asks.

blocks.q: Should I send a thank-you note?
blocks.a: Yes. Send a short, personal email to each interviewer within 24 hours. It reinforces your interest and keeps you top of mind.

blocks.text: Resume - Let's just get the obvious one out of the way. Set aside an hour or two to make some updates, edits, and tweaks, and get your resume where you want it. Remember, it's a brochure, not an autobiography. Efficient communication is valuable.

Social Media - Yep, it's important. Update your LinkedIn and ask past coworkers for LinkedIn recommendations. In addition, check your social media profiles. You don't have to use them in the job search (though you can), but you should at least make sure there isn't anything embarrassing posted. Most companies don't actively track down your social media, but better to make sure you're putting your best foot forward.

Portfolio - This is made up of examples of your body of work. For teachers, this is evidence of student achievement. For software engineers, this is Github. For web developers, this is web pages. For marketers, this is campaign and sales documentation. For academics, this is published papers. You get the idea; there's something for everyone. Struggling to find out what should go in your portfolio? Send me a message or comment below!

References - If you're looking for a new job, your references should be the first to know, not the last. Make sure you reach out, get an updated phone number and email address, and find out the best way for hiring managers to initiate a reference request when the appropriate time comes. Should they first email, call, or text?
Your Perspective - Essential Questions to Ask Yourself:
What don't you like about your current job? If you can't think of anything, why are you looking?
What do you like about your current job? If you can't think of anything, why do you show up to work every morning? And/Or, why have you stayed this long in this position?

What are the three most important characteristics you're looking for in your next job? If it's something logistical, like money or upward mobility, consider talking to your manager before you look outside of your current company. For all other characteristics, dig deep. "New challenges" means next to nothing to people who hear it all day (i.e. anyone who works in hiring). What kind of challenges? What are you hoping to learn in your next job? Why aren't you challenged in your current job?
Your Timeline - "Job Searching Is A Full Time Job":

Screening Calls - Once you switch your LinkedIn profile to "Open to New Opportunities" and post your resumes to job boards, people are going to reach out. You might get a good bit of spam, so be prepared to field those emails and calls. Mixed in there will be recruiters and hiring managers who looked at your profile and might be able to help with your job search. So, decide on your strategy to handle the traffic and avoid "throwing out the baby with the bath water."

Phone Interviews - Hiring managers are likely to have similar business hours as your current company. When are you going to have time to have time to step away to a private space for a 30-minute phone interview?
Final Interviews - When will you have time for a 4-hour onsite final interview? Do you have flexible hours? Do you have paid time off?

Start Date - The general standard across industries is 2 weeks. If that isn't the right fit for you, can you start right away? Do you have a project that you want to see through that ends in two months? What is your timeline?
#1: Establish your target field It’s marketing 101 – you should go as niche as possible. Applying to a wide range of positions and then using the same résumé doesn’t work.

#2: Research your target field Find out everything you can about the kind of role, company, and industry you are targeting and use this information to position yourself effectively by communicating your unique value proposition that addresses the needs of your target.

#3: Create a written plan If you don’t write things down, they don’t exist. If you don’t want to forget anything, I recommend you create a written plan and stick to it. This will keep you organized and on track.

#4: Address any gaps Determine where you have gaps in your experience, skills, knowledge, education, and other job requirements. Fill those gaps by taking courses, attending workshops/seminars, and/or volunteering in your target field.

#5: Create a branded résumé targeted for each job you apply to I can’t stress this enough – you must have a résumé that delivers your unique value proposition and that is tailored for each position you apply for. Don’t send the same document to multiple jobs, even if they are the same or similar. Each employer will have their own special requirements.

#6: Create a branded cover letter targeted to each job application 40% of hiring managers and recruiters expect a cover letter so it would be a great idea to create one. There are things you can address in a letter that you can’t in a résumé or Linkedin profile.

#7: Create a branded Linkedin profile If used correctly, Linkedin is a great tool to help generate interviews. But before you start reaching out to recruiters, hiring managers, and HR, you must create a strong, branded profile. There are various components of your Linkedin account that you need to optimize, giving special attention to the headline and 2000-character summary section.
#8: Assemble a portfolio of your work if you’re in a creative industry, it would make sense to bring along samples of your work that you’re proud of and that would be relevant for your target field.
If you’re a bit tech savvy, you could also create a personal website that has a section to showcase your work.

#9: Create your brag book Put together a list of all your key contributions and specific accomplishments that address the needs of your target field. This could be awards, accolades, surpassing targets – anything that demonstrates the kind of value you can bring to an organization. Keep a record of your accomplishments in a computer folder and update the list as required.

#10: Create a professional email address Set up a separate gmail address for your job search, that way it’s organized and emails don’t get lost with your other personal communication. Never use your current employer’s email address.

#11: Create a professional email signature The email signature is how you sign off at the bottom of your email such as Sincerely, John Smith, Business Development Manager. Make sure the job title you use is relevant and appropriate for the position you are targeting.

If you have a side hustle and you’re calling yourself the President/CEO, DON’T USE IT unless you’re targeting a President/CEO type of role. You don’t want people to reject you because you have positioned yourself a certain way (over or under-qualified) that doesn’t match your target field’s requirements and expectations.

#12: Record a professional voice mail message Keep your voice mail message clear, short, and highly professional. Do not insert any personal information into it that could be judged in a negative light.

Whatever phone number you publish, make sure that you are the only person answering it and not your 3-year old. It’s safer to stick with your personal cell phone and not a land line that everyone has access to.

#13: Reach out to 100+ hiring managers and network You should contact as many hiring managers as possible to generate informational interviews, discuss potential openings with them, and to get referrals. This is an important part of active networking. The most efficient way to do this is through Linkedin.
It’s a numbers game – the more companies you contact, the more you increase you chances of landing a job sooner than later.
#14: Email 100+ people you know Don’t forget to reach out to friends, family, acquaintances, former university/college classmates, people you know from social groups and networks.
The point here is to let them know you are looking for another opportunity and would appreciate it if they could spread the word and pass on your résumé (which you can attach).
The more people who know you’re looking, the better. Someone could know someone who’s looking for someone like you. I’ve known people who got jobs this way.

#15: Create 20 accomplishment stories Employers want to know the kinds of results (positive outcomes/solutions) you produced which is your value and goes beyond what your duties and responsibilities were. There is a difference!

Brain storm 20 accomplishment stories that are relevant to your target field and write them down. You need to quantify your contributions as much as you can by using dollars ($), percentages (%) and numbers/volume (#). Limit the stories you write to a paragraph or two that you can deliver verbally in about 90 seconds.

#16: Assemble ideal job postings Don’t focus on applying to jobs online because it doesn’t deliver great results but if you’re going to do this, you might as well apply to as many as you can. Keep track of applications on an Excel spreadsheet as not to duplicate efforts and stay organized so you can follow up.
#17: Research answers to the most common and dreaded interview questions You can google interview questions and answers. There are literally hundreds of them with the most common ones being:

Tell me about yourself, Why should we hire you? Why are you leaving your current position? What is your biggest weakness/strength? Why are you interested in this position? How much money are you looking for? What do you know about this company?

#18: Create your elevator pitches Create a short, medium, and long elevator pitch. This is your value summary a.k.a. unique value proposition or unique sales proposition. Your UVP is how YOU can solve whatever challenges the employer wants addressed.

Elevator pitches can be used for different applications such as your résumé, cover letter, Linkedin, personal website, and when you meet someone for the first time who asks you “So, what do you do for a living?”

#19: Create business cards Just because you don’t have your own “business” doesn’t mean you shouldn’t have business cards. You can hand them out to people you meet through professional networking events, socially, or standing in line at the grocery store. You never know who you’ll bump into, so it’s a good idea to be prepared.
#20: Create networking email templates Yes, you should be networking online (Linkedin) and even offline if it’s appropriate for you.

For Linkedin, you need to create different kinds of emails such as invitation requests, follow-up emails to new connections, and emails to existing connections. Since you’re saying pretty much the same thing to people, you can cut and paste the template and modify them accordingly.

#21: Set up a separate computer folder for each company you reach out to Place the job posting and accompanying résumé and cover letter in a folder that’s labelled the name of the employer. It’s better if everything’s in one place.

#22: Create a spreadsheet to track your job applications and follow-up If you’re networking, applying to jobs, and sending your résumé and cover letter anywhere you need to keep track of this activity to avoid duplicating efforts like contacting the same people more than once (which will be annoying for them).
#23: Create a spreadsheet to track your networking and follow-up Probably best to keep networking and informational meetings separate from actual job postings and applications.
#24: Use an online calendar to track meetings Use a google, Outlook, or some other calendar to organize your appointments so they’re available at a glance and you don’t miss anything.

#25: Determine and acquire suitable interview attire Make sure you have appropriate interview attire that’s been cleaned and pressed at least the day before so you’re not scrambling at the last minute.
#26: Have your job references ready While you should never put your references on your résumé or in the cover letter, you should have them typed up and standing by before you start your job search.

#27: Conduct salary research Salary negotiation is always the most stressful part of the interview process. Some employers or recruiters will ask you what you’re “looking for” during the initial phone interview.
You should research salary levels in your target field on various sites such as indeed, Ladders, Glassdoor, and Linkedin.
Another way is to talk to actual hiring managers who would be willing to give you that information. This will help you determine what your minimum acceptable salary range is.

#28: Clean up all of your social media The first thing the employer will do is google you to see what they can dig up in photos or posts about you that could be considered a “red flag”. You’ll need to to eliminate anything that could be construed as negative from all of your social media profiles (Facebook, Linkedin, Twitter, etc.)

#29: Prepare your questions for interviews You should prepare about 12 questions to ask the employer about the company and position. You won’t be able to answer them all, but you need more than enough in the event the employer addresses many of them during the meeting. You don’t want to be in the situation where they ask you “So, what questions do you have for me?” and you can’t come up with any.

#30: Prepare your questions for informational meetings Even if you are applying to jobs online, you should still generate informational meetings with hiring managers in your target field as part of your career research and networking efforts.

An informational meeting is NOT an interview and it is being grated as a favour, so keep it to 20 to 30 minutes max. You should prepare about 10 questions to ask the hiring managers but you might be able to ask only about 5 or 6.
#31: Determine what you’ll do when presented with a counter-offer Nothing can screw up your job search (and possibly your career trajectory) more than not knowing how to address a counter-offer.

#32: Develop and maintain a great attitude! If you lost your job recently or have been looking for a while, it can get pretty frustrating (and that would be an under-statement!) so it’s important to keep a positive mind-set. The people who are the most positive, persistent, professional, and proactive are the ones who land the jobs.

Who: members who entered service before January 1, 2018 and did not opt into BRS.
Formula: 2.5% × years of service × High-3. That is 50% at 20 years, 60% at 24, 75% at 30 (and up to 100% at 40 years).
High-3: the average of your highest 36 months of basic pay.
Paid: for life, starting the month after you retire, with a yearly COLA tied to inflation.
TSP: you can contribute, but there is no government match.
The catch: leave before 20 years and you get no retirement pay.
Who: members who entered on or after January 1, 2018, or who opted in during 2018.
Formula: 2.0% × years of service × High-3. That is 40% at 20 years, 48% at 24, 60% at 30.
TSP match: the government puts in 1% automatically from day 60, and matches up to 4% more after 2 years. Up to 5% of base pay a year, and you keep it even if you leave before 20.
Continuation pay: a one-time cash bonus, usually offered between 8 and 12 years of service, for agreeing to serve longer.
Lump sum option: at retirement you can take 25% or 50% of the present value of your retired pay up front, in exchange for reduced retired pay until age 67.
Paid: for life with a yearly COLA, same as High-3.

Retired pay = multiplier × years of service × High-3 (average of your highest 36 months of base pay). High-3 earns 2.5% per year and BRS 2.0%. The calculator caps the multiplier at 30 years (75% and 60%).
VA compensation is not paid while on active duty. Every year you stay, that tax-free check is part of what you give up.

Concurrent receipt (CRDP): at a 50% rating or higher, retirees with 20 years get full retired pay and full VA comp. Below 50%, retired pay is reduced dollar for dollar by VA comp, though the VA share is tax-free. Combat-Related Special Compensation (CRSC) may restore it.

All military pay counts: base pay, BAH, BAS, special and incentive pays, clothing allowance, CONUS COLA, bonuses, and the BRS TSP contribution. BAH, BAS, and clothing allowance are tax-free, so the calculator compares take-home pay, not gross pay.
Career head start: starting your civilian career later means a lower salary at every age until you stop working. The calculator counts that gap after tax.

True cost = take-home you give up while staying, plus the career head start you lose, minus the value of the bigger pension for the rest of your life. All amounts are valued at the day you would leave.

Civilian job security, career growth, and the head start on a second career and its retirement plan.

Security clearance value. Many cleared jobs pay a premium, and an active clearance makes you easier to hire.

blocks.q: What is the difference between High-3 and the Blended Retirement System?
blocks.a: High-3 pays 2.5% of your High-3 average base pay for each year of service, so 50% at 20 years, but nothing if you leave before 20. The Blended Retirement System (BRS) pays 2.0% per year, so 40% at 20 years, and adds government TSP contributions of up to 5% of base pay that you keep even if you leave early, plus continuation pay and a lump sum option at retirement.

blocks.q: Should I stay in the military after 20 years?
blocks.a: It depends on your numbers. Each extra year raises your retired pay by 2.5% of your High-3 (2.0% under BRS), but you give up a civilian salary, the retired pay you have already earned, and VA disability compensation, which is not paid on active duty. Starting a civilian career later also lowers your pay at every later age. Use our Stay or Go calculator to see your true cost.

blocks.q: Tell me about yourself.
blocks.a: What they want to know: A short summary of who you are professionally and why you are here. How to answer: Use present, past, future: what you do now, the experience that prepared you, and why this role is your next step. Keep it to 60 to 90 seconds. Veteran tip: Lead with your civilian-relevant title, not your rank. Example: "I led a 20-person aircraft maintenance team for six years."

blocks.q: Why do you want this job?
blocks.a: What they want to know: Whether you understand the role and are motivated by it. How to answer: Name two things about the role or company that genuinely interest you and connect them to your skills. Veteran tip: Say what draws you to the mission, then show how your service experience fits it.

blocks.q: Where do you see yourself in five years?
blocks.a: What they want to know: Whether you will stay and grow with them. How to answer: Describe growth in skills and responsibility that this role leads to. Avoid naming a different job or company. Veteran tip: Mention earning a certification or degree with your GI Bill if it fits the path.

blocks.q: What are your greatest strengths?
blocks.a: What they want to know: Self-awareness and fit. How to answer: Pick two strengths that match the job and prove each one with a short example. Veteran tip: Leadership under pressure, reliability, and attention to detail resonate when backed by specifics.

blocks.q: What is your greatest weakness?
blocks.a: What they want to know: Honesty and growth. How to answer: Name a real, non-critical weakness and what you are doing to improve it. Veteran tip: "I am still learning corporate tools like Salesforce, so I completed the free Trailhead courses."

blocks.q: Why should we hire you?
blocks.a: What they want to know: Your value compared with other candidates. How to answer: Summarize the top three ways you meet their needs in 30 seconds. Veteran tip: Combine experience, proven results, and a trait like mission focus.

blocks.q: Why are you leaving the military (or your job)?
blocks.a: What they want to know: Your motivation and whether there is a problem. How to answer: Stay positive and forward-looking: new challenges, growth, family, location. Veteran tip: "After 20 years of service, I am ready to bring my leadership to a civilian team."

blocks.q: Tell me about a challenge you overcame.
blocks.a: What they want to know: Problem-solving and resilience. How to answer: Use STAR and spend most of your time on the actions you took and the result. Veteran tip: Pick a story that does not require military jargon or classified details.

blocks.q: How do you handle stress and pressure?
blocks.a: What they want to know: Composure. How to answer: Describe your method (prioritize, communicate, execute) and give an example. Veteran tip: Deployments and inspections are strong examples if you explain them simply.

blocks.q: What are your salary expectations?
blocks.a: What they want to know: Whether they can afford you. How to answer: Give a researched range and say you are flexible for the right role and total package. Veteran tip: Research civilian pay; do not anchor to your military pay. Include clearance value if relevant.

blocks.q: What do you know about our company?
blocks.a: What they want to know: Whether you did your homework. How to answer: Share their mission, a product or contract, and a recent news item, then connect it to you. Veteran tip: Use the Company intel tool in our Career Command Center.

blocks.q: Describe your ideal work environment.
blocks.a: What they want to know: Culture fit. How to answer: Describe traits that match their culture based on your research. Veteran tip: Structure, teamwork, and clear goals translate well.

blocks.q: How do you handle conflict?
blocks.a: What they want to know: Teamwork and maturity. How to answer: Show that you address issues directly, listen, and focus on the shared goal. Veteran tip: Give an example of resolving a conflict between peers, not just enforcing rank.

blocks.q: What motivates you?
blocks.a: What they want to know: What keeps you engaged. How to answer: Tie your motivation to what the role offers: impact, learning, teamwork. Veteran tip: Service and mission are powerful motivators; link them to the employer's mission.

blocks.q: Do you have any questions for us?
blocks.a: What they want to know: Interest and preparation. How to answer: Always ask two or three questions about the role, team, and success. Veteran tip: "What does success look like in the first 90 days?" is a strong closer.

Is the VA home buying webinar free?

Active duty service members, veterans, National Guard and Reserve members, and military spouses and families. You do not need to be ready to buy yet.

A VA home loan is a mortgage benefit for eligible service members, veterans and some surviving spouses. It is made by private lenders and backed in part by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs.

Many eligible borrowers can buy with no down payment, depending on their entitlement and the lender's approval. The webinar explains how this works and what can change it.

Eligibility is based on your service history and is confirmed with a Certificate of Eligibility from the VA. The class walks through how to request one.

blocks.text: How to Answer "Where Do You See Yourself in 5 Years?"
Don't let this question scare you. Here's why they ask this in your interview:
They want to see if you've thought about your professional future
They want to make sure you're ambitious and hard-working

They want to make sure the job they're offering fits with your goals So, pick a work-related goal of where you’d like to be 5 years from now, and make sure it’s slightly challenging or ambitious. Nobody's going to tap you on the shoulder in 5 years and check if you hit these goals! You just need to say something that will make you sound motivated (but realistic).

So show you've thought about this topic, sound ambitious and motivated, but be realistic. Also make sure your answer is related to their job. They won't hire you if their job doesn't seem to fit your goals and plans. Example Answer: “I’m glad you asked. One of the reasons that I applied to this job was your company’s reputation for helping with its employees’ career growth and providing advancement opportunities. In the long term I see myself mastering the skills needed to do well in this role and then taking on more leadership responsibilities to continue growing my career here. I hope to become a manager later in my career.”
"Where do you see yourself in 5 years?"
Show ambition that fits their path.
They want to know you will stay, grow, and add value. Use this three-part formula.
Say you want to grow with a company like theirs
Avoid naming another job, company, or your own business plans
Name skills or responsibilities you want to build
Mention certifications you plan to earn, possibly with your GI Bill
Connect your growth to their goals and the team's success
"In five years, I see myself as a trusted leader on this team. I want to earn my PMP and take on larger projects, using the leadership I built in the Army to help the company grow."

blocks.text: How to Answer: "Why Do You Want This Job?

Employers want to hear specific reasons why you're attracted to their job. Why? They don't want to hire someone who sounds desperate, or doesn't care what type of job they want, because that person won't work as hard to learn the position and contribute great work. So the interviewer wants to hire someone who's motivated to do this specific type of work, and has thought about their career and goals. To answer, mention specific, work-related reasons why their job and company interest you. Focus mostly on the job. Talk about your own career goals and how this job fits those goals. Sound excited about the opportunity to work for them. Example Answer: “I’ve been actively searching for jobs since graduating with my Nursing degree. I’m interested in intensive care and emergency medicine and I’ve seen your hospital mentioned as having one of the best ER’s in the region. I thought the job description matched up well with my background, and saw some of my personal strengths mentioned, like multitasking and being able to thrive in a fast paced environment, so I’d love to begin my career here.”
Prove you chose them on purpose.
A great answer covers the role, the company, and you.
Name two duties in the posting that excite you
Explain why they fit your strengths
Mention their mission, product, customers, or culture
Reference something specific from your research
Connect your experience to their needs

"I want this role because it lets me keep supporting the mission I served for 10 years. Your work on [program] matters to me, and my experience leading logistics for a 300-person unit fits what your team needs."
